newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Sri Lankan battle toll surpasses 250-military.
newsitem.headline: Sri Lankan battle toll surpasses 250-military.

text.p: Sri Lankan troops scored a lopsided victory in the latest fighting with Tamil Tiger rebels in the northern Wanni region, which has now claimed at least 250 lives, the military said on Sunday.

A Defence Ministry statement said on Sunday that more than 200 Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE) rebels, many of them women, and 67 troops had been killed in the fighting that erupted late on Friday.

The ministry statement said troops clearing the affected area near Omanthai just north of the government-held town of Vavuniya, some 220 km (135 miles) north of the capital Colombo, had also recovered a large number of weapons left behind by the rebels.
The clandestine Voice of Tiger radio, monitored in Vavuniya on Sunday, however put the rebel death toll at only 89.
"This time they have got a big bashing," military spokesman Brigadier Sarath Munasinghe said earlier.
"It was a good blow to the LTTE. They did not expect this type of retaliation. The military was prepared," Munasinghe said.
The defence ministry said the LTTE launched seven assaults through Friday night but all of them were repulsed, causing heavy casualties to the rebels.
An LTTE spokesman in London said he had no information about the attack.
The military, which launched a major northward offensive in May, is battling rebels in the Wanni to open a strategic highway linking the northern Jaffna peninsula with the rest of the island.
The military's offensive -- and the fighting -- has slowed since the LTTE launched two fierce counterattacks in June, but the fighting has shown signs of escalating this week.
Sporadic fighting earlier in the week ended with the rebels launching their latest counterattack at Omanthai on Friday.
Diplomats said the Sri Lankan military was this time able to fill in breaches in defence lines caused by the assaults much more quickly than during the earlier attacks in June.
"They (the military) seemed to have got in reinforcements quickly to these areas. They were ready," the diplomat said.
But a former general, who led the Indian Peace Keeping Force (IPKF) in Sri Lanka a decade ago, said the latest offensive to open the highway seemed to have reached a stalemate.
"In one word I will describe it as a stalemate," retired general A.S. Kalkat said in an interview published in The Sunday Times.

Kalkat said the Sri Lankan army might be able to open the road, but added that it may not be in a position to carry out further offensive operations against the LTTE as most of the troops will be required to secure the road against rebel attacks.
"It is necessary to have this road as a safe continuous line of communication and maintenance...in which case it will have to controlled at all times and protected," Kalkat said.
He said the Sri Lankan military had deployed most of its troops in Jaffna to hold the peninsula, which was captured in April last year, leaving eastern areas open to the possibility of rebel attacks.
The LTTE have been fighting for a separate homeland for minority Tamils in Sri Lanka's north and east since 1983.
The government says more than 50,000 people have been killed in the war. The LTTE say the toll is higher.
